You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

name: arc-grid-rule-inference
description: Use when solving ARC grids from demos with limited actions.
---

# ARC grid rule inference under action constraints

Use this class-level workflow for ARC/Continual-ARC puzzles with demonstrations and a limited number of submissions or demo requests.

## Infer and verify
1. Parse dimensions, colors, candidate background/edge colors, markers, and action caps. Index cells consistently by row and column.
2. Compare each demo input/output at identical coordinates. Enumerate changed cells, their original and output colors, and unchanged structures. Separate marker recoloring from rays/fills and from wholesale stripe changes.
3. Maintain a small set of plausible rules. Consider orientation, anchor, extent, endpoint exclusion, target colors, and object interaction separately; do not infer from a single visual resemblance.
4. Replay every candidate on every demo cell-by-cell. Reject any rule that misses a changed cell or alters a preserved cell. A transformation is not validated merely because one part fits.
5. Apply the surviving rule to the test input, preserve unrelated cells, and validate dimensions, row lengths, bounds, and palette before submission.

## Demo/action budget
- A request costs score. Request only when a concrete ambiguity remains and explain internally which candidate rules the next example should distinguish.
- Use only actions authorized by the puzzle interface. In a submit/request_demos/finish protocol, do not call unrelated tools or task-planning actions; reason from visible grids and output only the required JSON action.
- After incorrect feedback, do not submit a near-identical grid with superficial edits. Treat the candidate rule as suspect, identify which assumptions were unproven, and reconstruct the output from the demos.
- If demos leave a behavior unresolved, do not present it as established. Seek a discriminating example only if worth its cost; otherwise make the most evidence-supported choice within the remaining attempt budget.

## Directional lines and boundary rays
For markers near edge bars, verify independently: ray direction, whether the marker becomes the ray color or a special color, where the ray stops, whether the boundary is preserved, and whether only marker-containing rows/columns activate. For diagonal rays, check each next cell: a current task-9bc5df6e run had rays extend through background to the boundary, but a test ray's next cell was a foreign non-background color and the accepted output preserved that blocker and added no ray. Thus use background-only extension when supported and never overwrite foreign-color cells without demo evidence. Other task-9bc5df6e recurrence had rays reaching boundaries; treat variant scope carefully. Do not assume opposite-edge symmetry. Special complete bands or stripes may have a separate selection rule; preserve them unless demonstrations establish how they are selected. See `references/boundary-ray-case.md` for a documented example and its limitations.

## Confirmed task-a8c517ee variant: fill enclosed frame interiors by parity
Two demos and an accepted test establish that outlined rectangular/square frames retain their borders while enclosed background cells are filled. The demonstrated outputs show fill color 2 when both interior dimensions are even (demo 2: a 2x2 hole; accepted test: a 6x6 hole), and color 7 when at least one interior dimension is odd (demo 1: 5x5; demo 2: 5x5, 5x7, 1x1, and 3x3; accepted test: 3x3 and 1x1). Other grid cells and frame borders stay unchanged. This parity mapping fits all observed cases. A further accepted 21x18 recurrence confirmed it: a color-4 frame with a 2x2 interior was filled with 2, while color-1 frame with 5x5 interior and color-8 frame with 1x1 interior were filled with 7; all frame borders and unrelated cells were preserved. Do not fill frame borders or globally recolor frame colors. Accepted test 15x20: the 4-frame at rows 0–7, cols 8–15 has 6x6 interior filled 2; the 5-frame at rows 9–13, cols 10–14 has 3x3 interior filled 7; the 6-frame at rows 10–12, cols 3–5 has its single interior cell filled 7. First submission incorrectly used 7 for the even 6x6 hole; accepted output confirms the parity mapping. A further accepted 23x22 recurrence has differently colored frames (colors 1, 4, 6, 8, 9) with 1x1, 2x2, 3x3, 3x2, 4x4 interiors. Fill 2x2 and 4x4 interiors with 2 because both dimensions are even; fill the others with 7 because at least one dimension is odd. The small 3x3 outer frames with 1x1 holes also receive 7. All borders, background (3), and unrelated content remain unchanged. This additionally confirms the rule is independent of frame color and applies to rectangular holes.

## Confirmed full monochromatic line recoloring variant: task-07cb84d7
A demo and accepted test establish that identify every row and column whose cells are all the same color, then recolor those complete lines to color 2. Keep all cells outside those qualifying lines unchanged; intersections are also 2. The line color need not match between lines. In the demo (21x28), complete color-1 rows (indices 1, 4, 14) and columns (indices 0, 5) became color 2; all partial/singleton color-1 cells and color-3 cells remained as-is. In the accepted 12x8 test, complete color-5 columns 2 and 3 and complete color-5 row 9 became color 2, while other 5s and all 7s stayed unchanged. Check full-line status against the original input, not incrementally modified cells. A further accepted 15x7 recurrence confirms the rule: the all-8 rows 2 and 14 and all-8 column 0 became 2; all other cells remained unchanged, including partial 8s. A further task-07cb84d7 recurrence with background 5 and line color 9 confirmed that every fully monochromatic row or column is recolored to 2, including all qualifying lines regardless of whether there is only one or several; in that 26x23 test, full rows 9 and 25 and full columns 9, 15, 18, and 22 were the qualifying lines. Validate by enumerating every row and column against the original input before generating output—missing even one full line causes a wrong answer. The rule is line-color agnostic: demonstrations also use monochromatic lines of colors 0, 3, and 5, all recolored to 2. Preserve every cell outside qualifying lines.

## Confirmed diagonal-residue periodic fill variant: task-fce33c1b
Sparse colored straight lines encode a periodic full-grid pattern: extend each marked line's color to every line with the same residue modulo the line period, producing a full tiled diagonal/stripe pattern. Determine the invariant coordinate (for example, `r+c` for up-right diagonals, `c-r` for down-right diagonals, or `r` for horizontal stripes), identify the period from parallel marker-line offsets, and map residue classes to their colors. Fill the entire grid from that residue-to-color mapping; this is not a sparse-line extension that preserves background.

Evidence from two demos and the accepted test establishes orientation-dependent cases. Demo 1 (21x21) used anti-diagonals of constant `r+c`, period 5, with residues 0..4 mapping to `[8,3,9,4,7]`. Demo 2 (23x23) used horizontal rows with period 2, row residue 0→2 and residue 1→1. Accepted 12x12 test used down-right diagonals of constant `c-r`, period 4, with residues 0..3 mapping to `[7,6,8,2]`, yielding rows `[7,6,8,2]`, `[2,7,6,8]`, `[8,2,7,6]`, `[6,8,2,7]` repeating. Infer the line orientation from marker geometry rather than assuming one axis; use line spacing and marker colors to complete residue assignments.

## Confirmed whole-pattern translation variant: task-3c7ebef4
A single demo and accepted 29x27 test establish that the complete sparse non-background pattern is translated down by exactly one row, preserving its columns and colors. The vacated top row is filled with the background color; the former last row is dropped at the boundary. Demo used background 8, pattern color 5, and output was precisely the input shifted down one row. Accepted test used background 3 and pattern color 9 with the same one-row downward shift. Infer the uniform translation vector from input/output demos, move the entire pattern as one shape, fill exposed cells with background, and clip at the grid boundary; do not change pattern geometry or recolor it.

## Output protocol
For strict ARC streams, emit exactly one valid action JSON object on the final line and no commentary. Ensure the grid has the required shape and only integer colors 0–9.

## Confirmed connector variant: task-63e6a38f
Color-2 marker cells on color-1 background are linked in straight horizontal and vertical lines: for each row and column, sort marker coordinates and recolor only the color-1 cells strictly between each consecutive pair to color 3. Keep marker endpoints, all non-gap cells, and unrelated background unchanged. No diagonal links or extension beyond the outermost marker. The demo and accepted 30x14 test both confirmed this behavior; simultaneous row/column links may cross, with linked cells color 3.

## Confirmed denoising variant: task-16b1bf1f
Three demos establish a noise-cleanup task. A dominant background surrounds coherent shapes/regions, with sparse singleton foreign-color pixels contaminating objects and background. Restore intrusions to the underlying object color or background; do not blanket erase all non-background colors. Demo1: bg1 and solid color6 shapes, noisy speckles 0/2/3/8/9; restore in-shape pixels and erase off-shape ones. Demo2: bg5, coherent color4 and color2 blocks; remove isolated 1/6/9 intrusions in blocks/background. Demo3: bg5 with coherent 7/8/9 structures; remove sparse 2/3/4/6 anomalies, preserving genuine rectangular objects. Accepted test solution kept coherent color1/color8 objects, turned speckles on objects back to object color (notably color8 object's anomalous notch at row 3 col7 0-indexed), and changed stray background specks to 0. Four guesses were wrong, mostly from failing to map speckles to either object or background precisely; distinguish structural holes/noise from intentional notches by cross-checking shape continuity and demos.

## Unresolved later run of task-21fede32
A distinct run with a 19x14 test ended with all 8 submissions wrong after 8 demos. Do not reuse a memorized answer from another run of this task id. The demos all showed a localized connected component being recolored, but neither component selection nor replacement color was resolved. Exact observed changes: demo 1, color-5 component at rows 1–3 cols 1–4 →6; demo 2, isolated 8 at (17,12)→9; demo 3, two 0 cells at row 28 cols 17–18 →4; demo 4, color-7 component row 4 cols 20–22 →8; demo 5, color-7 three-cell component rows 8–9 cols 25–26 →3; demo 6, six-cell color-2 component rows 13–15 cols 7–8 →5; demo 7, one larger color-8 component in central-lower area →7; demo 8, adjacent color-5 pair at row 6 cols 4–5 →8. These examples rule out simple global color substitution and a constant replacement color. Candidate submissions that recolored different test motifs (including the upper color-7 square, upper isolated 7, and color-8 objects) all failed; no submitted test transformation is evidence of the correct target. On any recurrence, map all demo components and their changed/preserved properties, and do not guess from shape/color resemblance alone. name: arc-lattice-corner-consensus
description: Use when ARC separator lattices encode values at crossings.
---

# Decode separator-intersection lattices

Use when a large ARC grid has regular horizontal/vertical separator lines with mostly uniform background along the lines, while small colored values appear at crossings. The output may be a compressed matrix over adjacent lattice faces.

## Verified evidence from task-47246f29

Three supplied demonstrations decode exactly by reading colored values at successive separator intersections. For each output cell, inspect the four corner crossing values from a 2x2 block of adjacent intersections: if all four crossing values are the same, output that color; otherwise output the interior panel/background color (3 in the demonstrated examples).

Demo 3 gives a clear cell-by-cell check. Lattice crossing rows are 8,13,18,23,28 and columns 4,9,14,19,24,29. Output is the 4x5 matrix for adjacent pairs of crossing rows/columns. E.g. the top-left 2x2 crossing block is all 0, so output 0; the next is all 0; mixed corners map to panel background 3; the bottom-right all-4 block maps to 4. This reproduces all 20 output cells. Demo 1 similarly produces a 4x6 matrix; demo 2's all-uniform lattice decodes to a single 8.

## Region selection resolved on task-47246f29

Do not assume a universal marker-only crop rule. Form faces between consecutive separator-crossing rows and columns, but use demos to determine the lattice span and whether edge crossings are included. Mixed corner colors map to the panel/interior background; unanimous four corners map to that shared color.

Fresh demo/test sequence validates full edge-inclusive lattice extent. Demo grid 27x23 had horizontal separator rows 1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22,25 and vertical separator columns 1,8,15,22. Crop crossings to rows 4..22 and cols 1..22, yielding 6x3 faces, with mixed cells becoming background 8. Test grid 24x28 had separator rows 0,5,10,15,20 and columns 0,6,12,18,24. The edge-inclusive lattice produced 4x4 faces, mixed cells background 2, and unanimous corners copied. Accepted output:
`[[2,2,2,7],[6,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2],[2,1,2,8]]`.

Older examples for this task showed other marker-based cropping; treat crop boundaries as instance-dependent and infer them from geometry plus demos, rather than assuming standout marker colors alone define the span.

## Method

1. Locate repeating full separator rows/columns and list their intersection coordinates.
2. Derive candidate output dimensions from adjacent intersections/faces, but test whether boundary rows/columns are clipped or only a subset is selected.
3. For each candidate face, read its four crossing colors. Compare uniform corners versus mixed corners; mixed faces may map to the panel background.
4. Replay the entire candidate output against every demo, including dimensions, before applying it.
5. If a test disagrees despite exact demo replay, treat it as evidence of an unmodeled selection or clipping rule; do not repeat near-identical outputs. Strict action interface: one JSON action only.

name: arc-striped-panel-pair-count
description: Use when stripes divide grids into sparse-marker panels.
---

## Edge-striped ray propagation variant (separate from panel counting)
For full-size grids with edge bars and sparse markers rather than panel partitions, demos may show edge-originating bands and horizontal marker rays. Treat this as a distinct task family, not the panel-counting rule: infer output color/direction and exact boundaries from demos, preserve unrelated cells, and avoid filling all edge-adjacent background automatically. In examples, 2 markers became 4 at ray sources and intermediate cells took the appropriate propagated color while an opposite-boundary edge cell remained unchanged. The edge-ray behavior needs demo-specific verification.

## Confirmed task-8e04f0ad variant: repeat bottom-band pattern across horizontal bands
A uniform full-width separator row partitions the grid into equal-height horizontal bands. In the demonstrated instance, the lowest band contains a sparse pattern on a field color; copy that entire band cell-for-cell upward into every band, preserving the separator rows. The copied pattern includes all colors and background-valued cells, not just sparse markers. Demo (9x5) had a separator at row 4, yielding three 4-row bands, with a sparse pattern in the lowest band; the output replicated that 4x5 pattern into the first and second bands while preserving the separator. Accepted test (20x7) had separators at rows 6 and 13, yielding three 6-row bands; its lowest band (rows 14–19) was copied into rows 0–5 and 7–12, preserving both separator rows exactly. Source/target bands were equal-sized in both cases. Validate the source band includes every cell/color and keep separators unchanged; do not infer a new sparse-marker rule.

# Striped panel pair-count decoding

Use when full-length uniform separator rows and columns divide a grid into rectangular panels. Panels contain a field/background color plus sparse cells of a distinct marker color, and expected output is a much smaller grid.

1. Locate complete uniform separator lines; treat them as dividers, not output.
2. Partition the area between dividers into panels. Output dimensions equal panel rows by panel columns.
3. Count sparse marker-color cells in each panel. In the demonstrated variant, output `1` when a panel has **exactly two** markers; otherwise output the panel's field/background color. Confirm colors and count rule from demos before applying.
5. Preserve panel order (top-to-bottom, left-to-right). Do not count divider cells.
6. Validate every panel against the demos, especially zero-, one-, and two-marker panels. Output the panel matrix, not the original grid size. Infer colors per instance, never hard-code example colors.

## Verified 2x2-panel variant
A confirmed instance used background 3, sparse marker 2, full separator rows and columns of 9, and 2x2 panels. Each panel became 1 iff it contained exactly two marker cells; a panel with one marker became background 3. A larger 5x4-panel demo confirmed the same exact-two rule, including panels with one or two markers. Thus the rule applies to panel marker counts, not panel dimensions or marker arrangement; count only cells inside each panel.

Demonstrations confirmed the same rule with different colors: a panel maps to 1 iff it contains exactly two sparse markers; otherwise it maps to its field color. Infer colors per instance, never hard-code example colors.

## Confirmed task-2442e88d recurrence: exact-two sparse marker panels
Full uniform separator rows and columns partition the grid into panels; emit one output cell per panel in top-to-bottom, left-to-right order. Across three demonstrations/test, a panel maps to output 1 iff it contains exactly two sparse marker cells; otherwise it maps to that instance's field/background color. Count only panel cells, excluding separators; panel dimensions and palette can vary.

Detailed recurrence evidence: Demo 1 input 19x14 had separator rows 4, 9, 14 and columns 4, 9 (0-indexed), making a 4x3 array of 4x4 panels. Background 9, marker 6, separator 2. The output was [[1,9,9],[9,9,9],[1,9,1],[9,9,1]]. Demo 2 input 17x5 had separator rows 5,11 and column 2, making a 3x2 panel array of 5x2 panels. Background 6, marker 7, separator 9. Output [[1,1],[1,6],[1,1]] confirms exactly-two rather than any-marker counting (the one-marker panel outputs 6).

Accepted test input 14x7 had separators rows 4,9 and column 3, yielding 3x2 panels with sizes 4x3/4x3 on first two panel rows and 3x3/3x3 on the last. Background 4, marker 7, separator 2. Panel marker counts were [[2,2],[2,2],[2,1]], and the correct output was [[1,1],[1,1],[1,4]]. Exclude all separator cells from counts. This recurrence independently confirms the rule with differing panel sizes, separators, and palette.

Further accepted task-2442e88d test recurrence: input 14x15 used full separator rows 4 and 9, and separator columns 3, 7, and 11, producing 3x4 panels. Background 4, sparse marker 8. The panel counts were [[2,2,2,2],[2,1,2,2],[2,2,1,2]], so the accepted output was [[1,1,1,1],[1,4,1,1],[1,1,4,1]]. This confirms the exact-two rule for four panel columns and panel heights 4, 4, and 4/3; a panel with exactly one marker maps to background 4.

A further accepted task-2442e88d instance had a 19x11 input with full separator rows 3, 7, 11, 15 and full separator columns 2, 5, 8, forming a 5x4 array of 3x2 panels. Background was 5 and sparse marker 8. The output was [[5,1,5,1],[1,1,1,5],[1,5,5,5],[5,1,5,5],[5,1,1,1]], confirming precisely two markers -> 1 and every other panel -> background, including panels with one marker and panels with more than two.

Another accepted instance had a 19x9 input with full separator rows 4, 9, 14 and separator column 4, forming 4x2 panels of 4x4 cells. Background was 4, sparse marker 7; exact-two marker counts by panel were [[2,2],[1,2],[2,1],[1,1]], and output was [[1,1],[4,1],[1,1],[4,4]]. The first test guess was incorrect because it used the wrong non-exact-two output color (5); the demo established that other panels retain the field/background color, not a fixed color. name: arc-task-variant-inference
description: Use when recurring ARC IDs may hide generated rule variants.
---

# ARC task variant inference

Use when an ARC/Continual-ARC task identifier has appeared before, or when a familiar visual pattern may conceal a new generated variant. A task ID and remembered solution are clues only; the current demonstrations are authoritative.

## Workflow
1. **Start fresh from the current instance.** Parse its input and demos. Do not copy a prior answer or assume task-ID recurrence guarantees the same rule.
2. **Inventory candidate structures.** Mark background, isolated markers, compact prototypes, connected objects, and all non-background offsets. Use a consistent anchor, usually a marker cell or the prototype bounding-box origin, and state offsets explicitly.
3. **Compare demo input/output at identical coordinates.** Record changed and preserved cells, including colors. Distinguish which objects act as anchors from the motif being copied; infer transparency of prototype-background cells rather than assuming it.
4. **Test complete rules.** Reconstruct the entire demo output from each candidate. A valid rule must account for every changed cell and preserve all unchanged structure, not merely explain a visually salient portion.
5. **Use prior knowledge only as a candidate generator.** Where a task ID has known variants, retrieve the relevant note in `references/variant-examples.md`, then decide from the current demo which (if any) applies. Never transfer a motif, anchor, orientation, palette, or target-selection rule without evidence.
6. **Spend demos selectively.** Request another example only for a specific unresolved ambiguity whose answer could change the test output. Avoid reflexive requests when the demo already identifies a unique rule. With a limited action budget, weigh demo cost against the risk of a wrong submission.
7. **Apply conservatively to the test.** Preserve unrelated cells, bounds-check all copied offsets, and validate row/column counts, dimensions, and color range before submitting.
8. **Honor the interface exactly.** In Continual-ARC action-only sessions, output exactly one permitted action JSON object, with no prose, and include a grid only for submission.

## Confirmed denoising variant: task-16b1bf1f
Three demos establish an image-noise cleanup task. The grids contain a dominant background and coherent solid/rectangular color regions; scattered singleton or isolated foreign-color cells are noise. Restore each noise pixel to the underlying coherent region/background color, but preserve coherent objects even when they have uncommon colors. Examples: demo 1 (27x10, bg1) removed scattered colors 0/2/3/8/9 and restored cells inside color-6 forms to 6; demo 2 (13x28, bg5) removed singleton intrusions 1/6/9 in coherent color-4 and color-2 regions, retaining the region colors; demo 3 (12x26, bg5) removed isolated 2/3/4/6 artifacts while preserving coherent 7/8/9 structures. Test output was accepted after replacing all isolated speckle colors with underlying bg/object colors: test bg0, retain color1 and coherent color8 structures, restore isolated noise intrusions (including 7/5/2/9 within 8 forms and stray nonzero cells on bg) to the local structured color or bg. Four prior submissions were wrong; correct output also changed an anomalous notch within a coherent color-8 object (row 3 col 7 in the 0-indexed test) back to 8. Do not merely erase noise to background: first determine whether each speckle lies on an object or on background. Preserve connected/block-shaped objects such as the 1 regions and 8 forms.

## Additional denoising variants observed: task-16b1bf1f
A 29x26 demo had background 9, solid rectangular/connected objects in colors 2 and 5, and color-4 speckles. Every isolated 4 was noise: 4 within a coherent object was replaced by that object's color; 4 on background was replaced by 9. Preserve the coherent object shapes, including small color-2 rectangles, and repair rather than blanket-erasing. For a test with other one-cell intrusions, the accepted output likewise kept coherent regions (4, 1, 5, 8) and repaired isolated non-region colors (2/9) to the underlying object or background.

A further accepted test had background 2, two coherent color-6 rectangular forms (3x3 and 5x6) and isolated contaminants of colors 0, 3, 4, 7, 8.
